chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Abu Ayyub al-Khazzaz, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I said to him: 'What is the matter with people who narrate from so-and-so and so-and-so, from the Messenger of God (may God's blessings be upon him and his family), and they are not accused of lying, yet something contrary to it comes from you?' He said: 'Indeed, the hadith is abrogated just as the Quran is abrogated.'

key_terms.خِلَاف: Contradiction/opposition — the narrator observes that the Imam's teachings sometimes contradict reports attributed to the Prophet.
key_terms.رَسُول اللَّه: The Messenger of God — referring to the Prophet Muhammad (SAWW).
key_terms.فُلَان: So-and-so — an anonymous placeholder in Arabic used to refer to unnamed persons without specifying identity.
key_terms.نَسْخ: Abrogation — the Islamic legal principle whereby a later ruling supersedes an earlier one. Applied here to hadith, not just Quran.

ai.seo_question: Why do the Imam's teachings sometimes differ from hadiths attributed to the Prophet?
ai.summary: Muhammad ibn Muslim, one of the most prolific companions of the Imams, poses a question to Imam al-Sadiq about an apparent contradiction: trustworthy narrators transmit hadiths from the Prophet, yet the Imam's teachings sometimes differ. The Imam resolves this by invoking the principle of abrogation (naskh) — just as later Quranic verses can supersede earlier ones, later prophetic hadiths can abrogate earlier ones. This teaching was essential for understanding the Shia hermeneutical approach to contradictory narrations, where the Imam's knowledge of which hadith abrogated which gives him an authoritative role in resolving such conflicts.
